title: Integrated Causal Reasoning Assessment: Bug Evolution
description: Assesses student understanding of natural selection, predator-prey dynamics, and the evolution of adaptive traits.

vignette.title: The Fast and Slow Beetles
vignette.text:
In a meadow, there is a population of beetles. Some beetles are naturally faster runners, while others are slower. Birds hunt these beetles for food.

When a bird attacks, faster beetles are more likely to escape, while slower beetles are more likely to be caught and eaten. However, being faster also requires more energy, so faster beetles need to eat more food to survive.

Over many generations, scientists observe that the average speed of beetles in the population changes. Sometimes the population becomes faster overall, sometimes slower, depending on the conditions.

context.setting: Meadow with beetle population and bird predators

items.question: If birds are very active and catch many beetles, what will most likely happen to the average speed of the beetle population over several generations?

options.text: The average speed will increase because faster beetles survive and reproduce more.
options.explanation: Recognizes that differential survival and reproduction (natural selection) leads to changes in trait frequencies over generations.

options.text: The average speed will decrease because the birds will eat all the fast beetles first.
options.misconception: Misunderstands selection - assumes predators eliminate the fittest rather than the less fit.

options.text: The average speed will stay the same because speed is not genetic and cannot be inherited.
options.misconception: Denies heritability of traits, a key requirement for natural selection.

options.text: The average speed will randomly fluctuate with no predictable pattern.
options.misconception: Ignores the directional pressure of natural selection.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding natural selection and differential reproduction

items.question: A student says: 'The beetles evolved to be fast because they needed to escape from birds.' What is the most accurate evolutionary response to this statement?

options.text: The student is correct - evolution happens because organisms need to survive.
options.misconception: Teleological thinking - assumes evolution has goals or purposes.

options.text: The student is wrong - beetles cannot evolve because they don't have intelligence.
options.misconception: Assumes evolution requires intelligence or conscious effort.

options.text: The statement is imprecise - faster beetles had higher survival and reproduction, so the speed trait increased in frequency over generations.
options.explanation: Corrects teleological language while accurately describing the mechanism of natural selection.

options.text: The statement is completely wrong - evolution is random and has nothing to do with survival.
options.misconception: Overcorrects to deny any role for selection in shaping traits.

items.question: If food becomes very scarce in the meadow, how might this affect the evolution of beetle speed?

options.text: Beetles will evolve to be slower because they don't need to escape birds if there's no food.
options.misconception: Assumes organisms can choose to evolve based on needs.

options.text: Beetles will evolve to be faster to catch the limited food more quickly.
options.misconception: Teleological thinking - assumes evolution has a goal of getting food.

options.text: The energy cost of being fast might become more important, potentially favoring slower beetles if they can survive with less food.
options.explanation: Recognizes that trade-offs (energy cost vs. predation risk) change with environmental conditions, affecting which traits are advantageous.

options.text: Food scarcity won't affect speed evolution because speed is only about escaping predators.
options.misconception: Ignores trade-offs and multiple selective pressures.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding trade-offs and multiple selective pressures

items.question: Scientists observe that in some meadows, beetles are very fast, while in other meadows with similar birds, beetles are much slower. What is the best explanation for this difference?

options.text: The fast beetles evolved more recently and are 'more advanced' than the slow beetles.
options.misconception: Progressionist thinking - assumes evolution has direction toward 'better' traits.

options.text: The meadows have different conditions (food availability, vegetation, etc.) that make different speeds advantageous.
options.explanation: Recognizes that adaptation is context-dependent - what's advantageous in one environment may not be in another.

options.text: The slow beetles haven't finished evolving yet - they will eventually become fast like the others.
options.misconception: Teleological and progressionist thinking - assumes evolution has a goal.

options.text: The birds in the slow-beetle meadows must be slower or less skilled at hunting.
options.misconception: Single-cause thinking - focuses only on predator traits rather than the full ecological context.

items.question: Can individual beetles choose to become faster or slower during their lifetime to better survive their environment?

options.text: Yes, beetles can exercise to become faster, just like humans can train to run faster.
options.misconception: Confuses individual learning/acclimation with evolutionary change.

options.text: No, individual beetles cannot change their inherited speed, but the population can evolve different average speeds over generations.
options.explanation: Correctly distinguishes between individual change (impossible for inherited traits) and population-level evolutionary change.

options.text: Yes, if a beetle needs to be faster, it will evolve to be faster within its lifetime.
options.misconception: Lamarckian thinking - assumes acquired traits can be inherited.

options.text: No, nothing about beetles can ever change - evolution is a myth.

integratedReasoning.description: Student understands natural selection as a population-level process with differential reproduction, avoids teleological thinking, and recognizes context-dependence.
indicators: Recognizes trade-offs and multiple selective pressures

dichotomizedReasoning.description: Student uses teleological thinking, progressionist assumptions, or confuses individual and population-level processes.
indicators: Assumes evolution has goals or direction

commonMisconceptions: Teleological thinking: 'Evolved to' or 'needed to' language
Lamarckian thinking: Acquired traits can be inherited
Progressionism: Evolution has direction toward 'better' traits
Individual-level thinking: Confusing individual change with population change
suggestedActivities: Run the model with different predation pressures and observe outcomes
Compare scenarios with high vs. low food availability
Discuss real-world examples of adaptation (antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance)
Use causal mapping to diagram selective pressures
connectionsToOtherModels: island-world: Explore how different environments create different adaptations
